problem: Existing embodied agents, whether RL/IL end-to-end policies or MLLM-based modular pipelines, act reactively and statelessly without structured, persistent spatial memory. Prior modular methods model only landmarks or only routes in isolation, which limits long-horizon navigation and spatial reasoning.
motivation: Biological spatial cognition consolidates landmarks, route knowledge and survey (map-like) knowledge, and retrieves them through visual-spatial working memory. The authors argue that MLLM agents need a comparable memory-centric design to generalize across goal modalities and granularities, and to support higher-level skills such as instruction following, EQA and mobile manipulation.
key_idea: Build a brain-inspired structured spatial memory (sparse landmark memory + dense voxelized DINOv2 cognitive map with surprise-driven updates) and query it with an MLLM-driven hierarchical working-memory retrieval, including imagine-then-localize via text-to-image generation, to give zero-shot universal navigation.
insight: Structured, persistent memory lets the agent localize goals directly instead of exploring reactively. It reaches high SR with few candidate locations, since most successful episodes succeed at the first explored coordinate (Supp. Fig. 2c). Combining landmark memory and cognitive map beats either alone (Supp. Fig. 2a). The distance+confidence ranking trades SR against SPL: extra explored candidates raise SR but lower SPL (Supp. Fig. 2d). Numeric ablation values appear only in figures.
method: Landmark memory: YOLO-World detects salient objects (conf. threshold 0.55). Each is stored as (category, 3D world coordinate from depth+pose, confidence, GPT-4o description). Duplicates within 1.0 m and of the same category are fused by confidence-weighted averaging.

Cognitive map: DINOv2 patch features are back-projected with depth and pose into 0.1 m voxels, each with a buffer of B=10 features. A surprise score (mean cosine distance to the n-hop neighborhood, threshold τ=0.5) decides insertion, and the lowest-surprise feature is replaced when the buffer is full (free-energy inspired).

Working memory, landmark retrieval: for simple category goals, a text-only GPT-4 reasons over the landmark list (labels, descriptions, confidences) to output up to K=3 candidate coordinates. It can infer unrecorded objects from co-located landmarks.

Working memory, association-enhanced cognitive-map retrieval: GPT-4o enriches goal text, Stable Diffusion 3.5 'imagines' images (3 per batch), and DINOv2 features are pooled with center-distance weights. Cosine top-K voxel matching plus similarity-weighted DBSCAN yields Q=3 candidates. Image goals query the map directly.
Exploration sequence planning: candidates are ranked by H = λ·p + (1-λ)(1-d/dmax) with λ=0.5, combining existence probability (confidence or similarity) and distance.

Low-level policy and verification: Habitat greedy shortest-path in simulation; A* on a LiDAR-SLAM occupancy grid plus TEB in the real world. At each candidate the robot does a 360° scan, CLIP picks the best view, and GPT-4o verifies the goal and outputs affordance adjustments.

Higher-level skills: GPT-o3 decomposes VLN instructions into waypoint subgoals. For A-EQA, GPT-4o answers at the reached location. GPT-4 generates waypoint-action sequences for real-world mobile manipulation.

setting.backbone: GPT-4/GPT-4o (frozen, retrieval/verification/description), GPT-o3 (instruction decomposition), YOLO-World, DINOv2, CLIP, Stable Diffusion 3.5-Medium (all frozen)
setting.training_data: none (training-free, zero-shot; pretrained foundation models only)
setting.action_space: discrete in simulation (forward 25 cm, turn ±30°, stop) via greedy shortest-path; continuous velocity commands (A*+TEB) on the real robot
setting.simulator: Habitat 3.0 (MP3D and HM3D scenes); real-world indoor environment
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration to build memory before each task (frontier exploration in sim, manual teleoperation in real world). Habitat scene-mesh greedy shortest-path follower for low-level actions in sim. Pose given.

numbers_note: Most quantitative results (SR/SPL for all baselines and BSC-Nav on TIN, SPL values for OGN/OVON/IIN, ablations) appear only in figures (Figs. 3, 4, Supp. Fig. 2), so these are omitted. TIN SR is described only as nearly double that of UniGoal/VLFM. Real-world results are per-target in figures, with a mean velocity of 0.76 m/s in the text.
results: BSC-Nav is zero-shot and beats UniGoal on OGN by +24.0 SR on HM3D (78.5) and +15.5 on MP3D (56.5). It also gets 71.4% SR on IIN (+11.4 over UniGoal) and nearly doubles UniGoal/VLFM on TIN. It reaches 38.5% SR / 53.1% SPL on VLN-CE R2R (8.5 SR below supervised Uni-NaVid but with higher SPL) and 54.6 LLM-Match on A-EQA (27.5 below humans). It also works on a real robot across 75 navigation episodes plus mobile manipulation demos.
limitations: Requires pre-exploration (frontier-based in sim, manual teleoperation in real world) to build memory before tasks, and the memory is mostly static, so dynamic or unstructured environments are unhandled.
Relies on many large foundation models (GPT-4/4o/o3, Stable Diffusion, YOLO-World, DINOv2), which is computationally costly and hard to run in real time. Verification uses repeated MLLM calls.
Significant gap remains to human performance in A-EQA. Many results are shown only in figures, and real-world evaluation is small-scale (15 targets, one 200 m² site).
